subject: Environment
sub_topic: ABS mechanism under Biological Diversity Act

concepts.name: Nagoya Protocol and its Incorporation into Indian Law
key_dimensions: Nagoya Protocol as the international legal basis for ABS under CBD — year of adoption (2010) and entry into force (2014)
How India's Biological Diversity Act 2002 predates Nagoya Protocol yet aligns with its principles — gaps and 2021 amendment attempts
Distinction between Nagoya Protocol obligations and what Indian domestic law actually implements — what is still missing
UPSC trap: Nagoya Protocol is under CBD, not a standalone treaty — its relationship with Cartagena Protocol on the same parent convention

concepts.name: Three-Tier Institutional Structure: NBA, SBBs, and BMCs
key_dimensions: Jurisdictional hierarchy — which body regulates which category of actors (foreign nationals → NBA; Indian industry → SBBs; local communities → BMCs)
UPSC trap: Overlapping jurisdiction — when does an Indian company need NBA approval vs. SBB approval (commercial use triggers SBB, not NBA, for Indian entities)
Composition differences: NBA is a statutory body under Central Government; SBBs under State Governments; BMCs are local self-governance units
Which body collects benefit-sharing fees and into which fund they flow — different funds at different tiers

concepts.name: National Biodiversity Authority (NBA): Powers, Functions, and Limitations
key_dimensions: NBA's prior approval requirement under Section 3 — who must seek it and for what activities (research, bio-survey, commercial utilization by foreigners/NRIs/foreign-controlled companies)
NBA's power to grant Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) approvals under Section 6 — critical ABS linkage with patent system
NBA as a quasi-judicial body — its power to impose penalties, compound offences, and its appellate structure
UPSC trap: NBA does NOT regulate every use of biological resources — Indian citizens for personal/local use are exempt; only certain commercial activities trigger NBA

concepts.name: Prior Informed Consent (PIC) Mechanism
key_dimensions: Who grants PIC in Indian ABS framework — NBA for foreign entities; SBBs for Indian companies; local community consent through BMCs for traditional knowledge
PIC vs. Prior Approval — subtle legal distinction: PIC is the consent of resource providers; prior approval is the regulatory permission
UPSC trap: PIC requirement for traditional knowledge holders (communities) is NOT always mandatory under current Act — a major criticism and gap
Comparison with Free, Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC) under Forest Rights Act — different legal standards for similar purposes

concepts.name: Mutually Agreed Terms (MAT) and Access Agreements
key_dimensions: MAT as the contractual foundation of ABS — what must be included: benefit-sharing mode, quantum, duration, and IP rights clauses
Role of NBA in approving/modifying MAT terms — it is not a passive regulator but can intervene in negotiations
UPSC trap: MAT is required even when PIC is obtained — both are independently necessary conditions for legal ABS
Consequences of accessing resources without MAT — civil and criminal liability under Sections 55–65 of the Act

concepts.name: Biodiversity Management Committees (BMCs): Role in ABS
key_dimensions: Mandatory vs. discretionary establishment — Section 41 mandates local bodies to 'constitute' BMCs; UPSC trap: it is the local body's duty, not NBA's
People's Biodiversity Register (PBR) — BMC's primary tool for documenting local biological resources and traditional knowledge as a basis for benefit claims
BMC's power to levy collection fees on commercial users — nature of this power and its limits (cannot exceed rates prescribed by SBBs)
Conflict between BMC decisions and SBB/NBA approvals — which authority prevails in case of dispute over access

concepts.name: People's Biodiversity Register (PBR): Legal Status and ABS Significance
key_dimensions: PBR as documentation tool vs. legal protection instrument — it records but does NOT automatically create legal rights or prevent biopiracy
UPSC trap: PBR is NOT a patent or sui generis protection — it is only prima facie evidence of prior knowledge; still vulnerable to third-party IPR claims
Role of PBR in triggering benefit-sharing obligations — if a resource/knowledge is in PBR and commercially accessed, benefit sharing with that community is triggered
Challenges: Incomplete PBRs, lack of digitization, language barriers — policy criticism angle for Mains

concepts.name: Sections 3, 4, and 6 of Biological Diversity Act: The ABS Trigger Provisions
key_dimensions: Section 3: Restriction on access by foreign nationals/entities — prior approval of NBA mandatory for biological resources OR knowledge associated
Section 4: Restriction on transfer of research results to foreigners — often overlooked but critical; NBA approval needed even for sharing research data
Section 6: IPR application restriction — any person applying for IPR based on biological resources must obtain NBA approval BEFORE applying — UPSC trap on sequence
Comparison: Section 3 covers access; Section 6 covers downstream IPR — both are ABS-linked but at different stages of the value chain

concepts.name: Exemptions from ABS Provisions: Who is Outside the ABS Framework
key_dimensions: Section 7 exemption for Indian citizens — local communities, growers, vaids, hakims using resources for personal/medicinal/local trade NOT subject to SBB approval (only intimation needed)
UPSC trap: Section 7 exemption applies to SBB approval, NOT to NBA — foreign-controlled Indian companies still need NBA even for same activities
Collaborative research exemption under Section 5 — government-approved collaborative projects between Indian and foreign institutions have a modified ABS pathway
Cultivated varieties and agricultural biodiversity — partly outside BD Act; governed by Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act (PPVFRA), creating a jurisdictional overlap

concepts.name: Benefit Sharing Mechanisms: Monetary and Non-Monetary Forms
key_dimensions: Types of benefits: upfront payments, royalties, milestone payments, technology transfer, capacity building, co-authorship — Nagoya Protocol's Annex I list
India's practice: NBA-determined benefit-sharing percentage deposited into National Biodiversity Fund — communities often receive indirect benefits, not direct payments
UPSC trap: Benefit sharing goes to NBA/National Biodiversity Fund first, then to communities — NOT direct payment to resource providers in most cases
Criticism: Long delay and opacity in fund disbursement to local communities — governance failure angle

concepts.name: National Biodiversity Fund and State Biodiversity Fund
key_dimensions: Composition of National Biodiversity Fund: fees from NBA approvals, grants from Central Government, penalties collected — Section 27
Utilization of fund: conservation of habitats, socio-economic development of local communities, ex-situ conservation — NOT solely for benefit sharing
UPSC trap: State Biodiversity Fund is separate from National Biodiversity Fund — managed by SBBs for state-level ABS collections
Accountability gap: No mandatory timeline for disbursement to communities; CAG has flagged underutilization of funds

concepts.name: ABS and Traditional Knowledge: Interface with Intellectual Property Law
key_dimensions: Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) as a defensive protection mechanism — not under BD Act but complements it by preventing grant of patents on documented TK
Section 36(5) of BD Act — obligation of Central Government to protect traditional knowledge through measures including legislation (enabling provision, not self-executing)
UPSC trap: TKDL is managed by CSIR/AYUSH Ministry, NOT by NBA — different institutional home for TK protection vs. ABS regulation
Sui generis protection gap — India lacks a dedicated TK protection law; BD Act + TKDL + Geographical Indications Act together provide partial protection

concepts.name: Biopiracy: Definition, Notable Cases, and Legal Remedies under BD Act
key_dimensions: Biopiracy definition in ABS context: unauthorized access and commercialization of biological resources/TK without PIC and MAT and without sharing benefits
Notable cases: Neem (EPO patent challenged), Turmeric (USPTO patent revoked), Darjeeling Tea (GI protection) — each illustrates a different legal remedy
UPSC trap: BD Act 2002 came AFTER most famous biopiracy cases — Neem and Turmeric cases were resolved using prior art arguments, NOT BD Act provisions
NBA's role in challenging patents: Section 18(4) empowers NBA to oppose IPR grants in India and abroad — rarely exercised in practice

concepts.name: Compliance Mechanism and IRCC (Internationally Recognized Certificate of Compliance)
key_dimensions: IRCC under Nagoya Protocol: issued when PIC is granted and MAT established — published on ABS Clearing House as proof of legal access
India's obligation to issue IRCCs and report to ABS Clearing House — implementation status and gaps
UPSC trap: IRCC is a Nagoya Protocol instrument; India's BD Act does not explicitly mention IRCC — it must be read into Section 3/4 compliance
ABS Clearing House (ABSCH) as the global transparency mechanism — role in tracking compliance and preventing misappropriation across jurisdictions

concepts.name: Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act 2023: Changes to ABS Framework
key_dimensions: Key change: AYUSH sector practitioners, local communities, and codified traditional knowledge users exempted from benefit-sharing obligations — Section 7 expanded
Controversy: Critics argue 2023 amendment weakens ABS by exempting large AYUSH industry players who commercially exploit TK at scale
Change in NBA's role: More facilitative than regulatory for domestic industry — shift in philosophy from conservation-centric to industry-friendly
UPSC trap: 2023 amendment does NOT remove NBA's power over foreign entities — Section 3 restrictions on foreigners remain intact; only domestic exemptions widened

concepts.name: ABS Clearing House (ABSCH) and India's Reporting Obligations
key_dimensions: ABSCH as the international information-sharing platform under Nagoya Protocol — what countries must publish (PIC decisions, MAT, checkpoints, IRCCs)
India's compliance: Partial reporting; not all NBA approvals are reflected in ABSCH — sovereignty concerns vs. transparency obligation tension
Checkpoint mechanism: Customs, patent offices, and research institutions as 'checkpoints' to verify legal provenance of biological resources
UPSC trap: ABSCH is under Nagoya Protocol/CBD Secretariat, NOT under UNEP directly — common confusion in questions about institutional homes

concepts.name: Relationship Between BD Act and Other Domestic Laws: Jurisdictional Overlaps
key_dimensions: BD Act vs. Forest Rights Act: Both protect community rights over biological resources in forests — FRA gives ownership rights; BD Act gives benefit-sharing rights — different but complementary
BD Act vs. PPVFRA: Farmers' varieties and wild relatives — PPVFRA governs farmers' rights over plant varieties; BD Act governs access to wild biological resources; overlap in landraces
BD Act vs. Patents Act: Section 10(4)(d)(ii) of Patents Act requires disclosure of biological material source — this links patent prosecution to BD Act compliance
UPSC trap: Violating disclosure requirement under Patents Act does NOT automatically mean BD Act violation — separate penalties under separate statutes

concepts.name: Scheduled Tribes and Local Communities as Benefit Claimants: Rights and Gaps
key_dimensions: Who qualifies as 'local community' under BD Act — not defined precisely; broader than 'Scheduled Tribe' under Forest Rights Act — UPSC definitional trap
Collective rights vs. individual rights in benefit sharing — BD Act contemplates community-level benefit sharing, not individual; implementation challenge
Grievance redressal mechanism for communities: No dedicated tribunal — communities must approach NBA or civil courts, making access to justice difficult
Gender dimension: Women as primary knowledge holders of biodiversity — BD Act is gender-neutral but Nagoya Protocol's Bonn Guidelines recommend gender-sensitive ABS

concepts.name: Penalties and Enforcement under BD Act: ABS Violations
key_dimensions: Section 55: Penalty for contravening Section 3 (foreign access without approval) — imprisonment up to 5 years OR fine up to 10 lakh or both — cognizable and non-bailable
Section 57: Compounding of offences — NBA can compound (settle) offences for first-time violators; UPSC trap: not all offences are compoundable
Enforcement gap: No dedicated enforcement agency; NBA relies on state police and forest departments — practical implementation weakness
Comparison with Wildlife Protection Act penalties — WPA has stricter enforcement machinery (Wildlife Crime Control Bureau); BD Act lacks equivalent

concepts.name: Digital Sequence Information (DSI) and the Frontier ABS Challenge
key_dimensions: DSI definition: Genetic sequence data stored in databases (GenBank, BOLD) derived from biological resources — does ABS apply to DSI? Major unresolved question
Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (2022): Agreed to establish multilateral benefit-sharing mechanism for DSI — India's position supporting DSI inclusion in ABS
UPSC trap: India's BD Act 2002 does NOT explicitly cover DSI — it covers 'biological resources' and 'knowledge' but sequence data in databases is a grey area
Implications: If DSI is excluded from ABS, genetic resources can be digitized and used commercially without benefit sharing — effectively circumventing the entire ABS framework
